chapters.cast-step-0: Step 1: The data that has to survive
chapters.cast-step-1: Step 2: Copy it to a second machine
chapters.cast-step-2: Step 3: The backup machine has it

events.text: Start with the thing that has to survive. Inside the live repository there is a file holding a single order line. Keep an eye on it, because we are about to take this machine offline and get that line back from somewhere else.
events.afterText: That is the line. Everything from here is about getting it back.
events.prose: Read the payload out of the live repository first. One line in one file, so the proof at the end is something you can see rather than something you have to take on trust.

events.text: Copy the whole repository to a second machine. The first copy carries the entire encrypted image over SSH, about two gigabytes in half a minute here. What lands on the other side is a backup artifact, not a second running app.
events.afterText: The copy is on the backup machine now.
events.prose: Copy the repository to a second machine. The first push carries the whole encrypted image, roughly two gigabytes in thirty to forty seconds on this fleet, and every push after it sends only the blocks that changed. What lands on the target is a backup artifact rather than a second live repository.

events.text: Ask the backup machine what it is holding. The repository is there under its own name. The second row, the one showing a raw identifier, is the retained base that lets the next push send only what changed.
events.afterText: Both rows are expected: the copy, and the base that keeps later pushes small.
events.prose: Ask the backup machine what it is holding. The copy appears under its own name, resolved from your config. The second row carrying a raw identifier is the retained delta base, which is what makes the next push to this machine incremental.

events.text: Now the disaster. Stop the primary and unmount its encrypted volume. As far as this machine is concerned, the application is gone.
events.afterText: Down and unmounted. Everything after this runs against the copy.
events.prose: Take the primary offline: stop its services and unmount the encrypted volume. Everything from here runs against the copy on the other machine.

events.text: Turn the artifact into a running repository. Restore is the verb that does it. One flag names the new repository, one places it on the backup machine, and one skips the confirmation.
events.afterText: The copy is a repository now, under a name of its own.
events.prose: Restore is the verb that turns a pushed copy into a repository. It is named with --as, placed with --machine, and confirmed with --yes. Restoring under a new name overwrites nothing, which is what makes this safe to practise on a live machine.

events.text: Mount the restored repository. We are deliberately not starting its containers, because the proof we want is the data, not the application.
events.prose: Mount the restored repository. The containers stay down on purpose: the thing being proved here is the data, not the application.

events.text: The same command we ran at the start, against a repository that did not exist two commands ago. Same file, same line, same order.
events.afterText: That is the whole point. The data came back.
events.prose: The same command as step one, run against a repository that did not exist two commands ago. The line comes back byte for byte, out of a machine that was never the original.

events.text: One more, for backups you can roll back through. Snapshots go to the chunk store, where the first run uploads everything and every run after it uploads only the blocks that changed. Any snapshot restores on its own. It needs an account and a licensed repository, so here it is typed rather than run.
events.afterText: Type it on your own installation once you have an account, and it will run.
events.prose: Copying to a machine gives you the repository as it is now. For a history you can roll back through, snapshots go to the chunk store: the first run uploads the written blocks, every run after it uploads only what changed, and any snapshot can be restored on its own. This one is typed and not run, because uploading needs an account server and a licensed repository, neither of which a recording has. On your own installation, with an account, this is the command.

narrations.text: Your app is live, so let's make sure you never lose it! In this tutorial we copy a whole repository to a second machine, take the first one offline, and bring the data back.
It comes down to three steps. Copy the repository to a machine you control, restore that copy into a repository of its own, and then prove it by reading your data back out.
Your data is safe and portable across machines. See you in the next one!
